paper_title: Review without a queue: what Chen and Stratton (2026) mean for an autonomous system
paper_frame: We map each of their findings to the mechanisms Ultrastable uses instead of a human review queue, and test each mapping against this system's own records.
title: Artificial Intelligence in the Firm: Bottlenecks in Software Production
kind: job market paper (working paper, not peer reviewed)
data: 445M work events (GitHub, Jira, Google Calendar) for 720,542 workers at 655 firms, January 2021 to August 2026, from an engineering analytics platform; staggered difference-in-differences on AI tool adoption timing
summary: AI coding tools raise code output substantially but final software output only a little, with no detectable employment effect. Code review becomes the bottleneck: code waits longer for a reviewer, spends longer in review and draws more requested changes.

findings.concern: More code is not more shipped work
findings.claim: After AI agent adoption, pull requests opened rise 35.7% while resolved issues (work deployed to production) rise only 13.7%; increases above 30.7% are ruled out.

mechanisms.how: the system's own score counts verified live deploys, never commits or lines
the public progress page lists merged and shipped work only; record-keeping merges are excluded

findings.claim: After AI agent adoption, the time from a pull request's submission to its merge rises 56.1%: waiting for a reviewer rises 59.9% and time in active review 58.5%.

mechanisms.how: a server-side lane merges a green pull request without waiting for a person
the tick Worker owns merge, deploy and live verification after a pull request opens
a green pull request left open fails a check

findings.concern: System-made changes wait longer than session-made ones
findings.claim: The study's model predicts that when review capacity is fixed, the waiting time grows with the volume of submitted code. A system that writes its own changes must not let its own pull requests queue behind human-driven ones.
findings.where: Model, propositions on backlog and wait time

mechanisms.how: the lane takes every open pull request until none is left
work the system originates on itself is ranked first when the regime is driven

findings.concern: Lower code quality raises review effort and risk
findings.claim: After agent adoption the share of changes receiving a review comment rises 13.1% and comments per change rise 38.6%; interviewees report outages caused by AI-generated commits.

mechanisms.how: a model change that elides or stubs code is refused before it becomes a pull request
a red main is repaired by reverting the smallest change that broke it
every failure mode has a live detector and a queue item

findings.claim: Code must be reviewed and tested before it can be deployed; the study treats review as the quality gate that AI-written code strains.

mechanisms.how: every deploy runs a verify line against production and rolls back on failure
freshness of each live source is served and probed

findings.concern: AI review tools leave humans in the loop
findings.claim: 79.1% of firms adopted AI code review tools, but the overwhelming majority of reviews and comments are still written by people, so the bottleneck persists.

mechanisms.how: no step waits on a person reading, reviewing or approving
human touches are counted every tick and lower the score

findings.concern: One approver is a single point of failure
findings.claim: Reviewers mostly review code they already know (82.8% versus 17.2% at random); an interviewee describes one senior engineer as the only approver, reviewing once a week.

mechanisms.how: every single point of failure, approvals included, is registered and remediated
every merge and deploy path has a second route needing no person's credential
